summary: Discusses when IETF protocols can be extended with little or no review and when extensions need community review. Experience shows that unreviewed extensions can cause interoperability and architectural trouble. This is a Best Current Practice.

plainLanguage.summary: If everyone adds their own parts to a toy without telling anyone, the pieces may not fit. This note says when you can just add things and when you should ask the group first.

questions: when should protocol extensions be reviewed
what is the difference between a protocol extension and a variation
how do vendors extend ietf protocols
can i just pick a codepoint for my extension
subtitle: Guidance for vendors and other standards bodies on when and how to get IETF review before extending an IETF protocol.

tldr.problem: Vendors and other standards bodies sometimes extend IETF protocols on their own, and extensions made without understanding the base protocol can break security, congestion control or interoperability.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC explains the technical risks, says that significant extensions need early technical review, and lays out routes for getting it: the normal IETF process, an IRTF Research Group, or an Independent Submission to the RFC Editor.
tldr.outcome: It is a Best Current Practice aimed mainly at other standards bodies and vendors, and it does not change formal IETF processes.

today: RFC 4775 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 125). It has not been obsoleted or updated according to the metadata, so it remains the IETF's published guidance on this topic.

sections.title: Why Extensions Need a Procedure
sections.content:
IETF working groups usually build ways to extend a protocol into the design, because a successful protocol is often one that is used in ways nobody planned. Still, the RFC says experience shows that extensibility features should be limited to what is clearly necessary, and that later extensions should be made carefully, with full understanding of the base protocol, existing implementations and current operational practice.

The question the RFC answers is how other Standards Development Organizations (SDOs), vendors and technology fora should proceed when they need an extension to an IETF protocol. It is directed principally at them and does not modify formal IETF processes. It also says the IETF claims no special position: everything it says would apply equally to protocols specified by any SDO.
sections.plainLanguage: When lots of groups share one set of rules, someone who wants to add a new rule should ask the people who wrote the original ones. This note explains how to ask.

sections.title: Technical Risks in Extensions
sections.content:
Extensions made without full understanding of the existing protocol can repeat ideas that were already considered and rejected, or can unintentionally negate key functions such as security or congestion control. Independently developed extensions may also turn out to be incompatible with each other.

Documentation of non-IETF extensions can be hard to obtain, so checking the quality of the specification and its compatibility with other extensions may be hard or impossible. A set of interrelated extensions to several protocols carries a greater danger than a single extension and should get earlier and more in-depth review.

The RFC also separates two ideas. An extension adds features and, if well designed, lets old and new implementations interoperate. A variation modifies features so that old and new implementations may not interoperate. Variations must be intensely scrutinized, and everything said about extensions applies to them as well.
sections.plainLanguage: A new part that is added carefully still fits the old toy. A part that changes how the old pieces work might not fit at all, so it needs an extra close look.

sections.title: Interoperability, Registries and Review
sections.content:
The IETF designs protocols for the single Internet and expects them to work the same everywhere. Extensions for limited environments can be reasonable if products with the extension still interoperate with products without it. Extensions that break interoperability are unacceptable when the two are mixed, and the RFC says this tends to happen on the Internet even when designers did not expect it.

New values for an extension often go into an existing IANA registry, and the RFC says they must be registered by the applicable procedures. Designers sometimes assume a codepoint is theirs for the asking, or for the taking, which is hazardous: the same value may later be formally assigned to another function.

The RFC treats the split between minor and major extensions as a matter of judgment. A new TLV in an application protocol might be minor, while a new IP option type, which could affect every node, is major. The only safe rule is that early review by subject matter experts is advisable even for an apparently minor extension. Merely registering a value in a First Come First Served registry is not intended to require formal IETF review.

A proposed extension should also be documented in a clear specification that experts can review, ideally as an Internet Draft written consistently with the unextended specification.
sections.plainLanguage: If you scribble a number on a locker without checking, someone else may be given the same locker later. Ask the person who hands out the lockers first, and have someone who knows the building look at your plan.

sections.title: How to Get an Extension Reviewed
sections.content:
The RFC lists three ways an extension can be considered for publication as an RFC:

  • Extensions developed within the IETF go through the normal IETF process, like new designs.
  • Extensions discussed in an IRTF Research Group may be experimental before the work is mature; the group must involve appropriate IETF or IANA experts.
  • Extensions in Independent Submissions to the RFC Editor get IESG review under BCP 92 (RFC 3932). Independent Submissions cannot be placed on the IETF Standards Track.

A vendor or SDO should first check whether the need is straightforward and within a documented extension mechanism. If so, that mechanism must be followed. If not, the next step is to contact the relevant IETF Area Director to find out whether there is an active working group or at least relevant expertise. If the IETF no longer has the expertise, the choices are to bring the work to the IETF or to agree that the IETF exports change control.

A standards process within the IETF, with appropriate liaison, is strongly recommended over publishing a separate non-IETF standard, which would split the standard into parts from different sources with no unitary control. SDOs are encouraged to talk to the IETF as soon as an idea is well formulated, so that the IETF is not handed a fait accompli. Vendors are strongly recommended to start informal discussion and publish a preliminary Internet Draft. A vendor with a proprietary extension that draws no IETF or IRTF interest is pointed to an Independent Submission rather than a proprietary document.
sections.plainLanguage: First check the rule book for a built-in way to add things. If there is not one, talk to the people in charge early, before you have spent months building something they might not accept.

sections.title: If You Publish Anyway, and Special Cases
sections.content:
If a vendor or SDO publishes its own extension specification despite the recommendations, the guidance is that it should be well and publicly documented and reviewed early by the IETF community. Such publications are formally requested to be submitted for IETF review, through a liaison channel if one exists, or else by asking the IESG or an Area Director. Security, internationalization and management may need review as well as the protocol itself. The publication must also include an IANA Considerations section, so that parameter assignments are not made until the extension has been adequately reviewed. For routine IANA assignments covered by an existing IANA Considerations section, the request is satisfied if those considerations are met.

Section 5 of the RFC covers specific cases. MIB modules are often defined outside the IETF, and BCP 111 (RFC 4181) gives guidance. Experimental values reserved in some registries are not meant for production use or to evade review (see RFC 3692 and RFC 4727). New RADIUS attributes should involve IETF experts, since adding them without discussion creates a high risk of interoperability or functionality failure. Documents that set change processes for specific protocols, such as SIP (RFC 3427), are not overridden.
sections.plainLanguage: If you build your own add-on anyway, share the plans in public and let the experts check them. Do not use the practice-numbers meant for experiments as a way to skip the checking.

sections.title: Security, IANA and Intellectual Property
sections.content:
The security consideration is short: an extension must not introduce new security risks without also providing an adequate counter-measure, and it must not inadvertently defeat security measures in the unextended protocol. This must always be considered during IETF review.

The IANA section asks IANA to pay attention to this document's requirements when asked to make protocol parameter assignments for vendors or other SDOs, and to respect the IANA Considerations of all RFCs that contain them and the general considerations of BCP 26 (RFC 2434).

On intellectual property, all IETF documents fall under BCP 78 and BCP 79, so anyone outside the IETF considering an extension based on an IETF document must keep the legal restrictions on derivative works, and the rights remaining with the original authors, in mind.
sections.plainLanguage: A new add-on must never switch off a lock that the original toy had. And copying someone's rule book has its own rules.
